Name: Håkon Hapnes Strand
Question: Is it correct for a single team to own multiple microservices?
Answer: There is no “correct” way to design software systems. That's the beauty of it. It's more art than science. I've been involved in a small (3–4 devs) team that owned 14 microservices. I've also been the sole developer on a codebase that spanned multiple microservices. Currently, my team is running a complex multi-tenant B2B SaaS solution as a monolith. So everything is possible. One microservice per team can be a good organizational architecture, since physical separation of concerns can reduce friction between teams. However, that's not to only reason split a system into microservices. Perhaps different parts of the solution has different scaling requirements. Perhaps you want to use different programming languages. Perhaps you need stronger fault isolation to improve reliability. And so on. There is no catch-all architecture that works in every case. You need to consider the unique requirements of each system.

Name: Håkon Hapnes Strand
Question: What is the role of software architecture in large-scale projects?
Answer: Software architecture is just a fancy word for any part of the design of a software system that is on a higher abstraction layer than the code itself. If your software system has several modules split up by logical or technical boundaries, the way you compose these modules and enable them to interact is called architecture. Choice of technical infrastructure, programming languages and frameworks can also be considered architecture. The way your system interacts with other systems, or even the way it's embedded in an organization, can be considered architecture. The role of a software architect, then, is to design the software system at a high level such that it meets the requirements efficiently. A well-functioning software development team doesn't really need to appoint an architect. The natural leaders and architects will emerge by merit.

Name: Håkon Hapnes Strand
Question: According to Nvidia CEO Jen-Hsun "Jensen" Huang, coding is dead. Do you agree?
Answer: Of course it's not dead. There are tens of millions of people around the world who are paid to write code on a daily basis. They are paid well too. Jensen said that kids shouldn't learn to code. While I understand his motivations and I agree with him that AI is going to transform the way we program computers, I still think it's an irresponsible thing to say. The world will still need software engineers for the foreseeable future, even if AI is going to gradually take over more of the programming work. Any young person today who is interested in computer science should study it and learn how to write code. There will be work for them in the future, even if the job might not look exactly like the same as it does now.

Name: Håkon Hapnes Strand
Question: Has any human player been able to consistently beat the level 25 bot on chess.com?
Answer: I’m guessing the engine behind the level 25 (3200 Elo) engine is actually Stockfish 11, which is used at chess.com to analyze games. If my assumption is correct, that bot is basically unbeatable for humans. It’s an older version of Stockfish, but not that old. From the release notes: This version 11 of Stockfish is 50 Elo stronger than the last version, and 150 Elo stronger than the version which famously lost a match to AlphaZero two years ago. This makes Stockfish the strongest chess engine running on your smartphone or normal desktop PC, and we estimate that on a modern four cores CPU, Stockfish 11 could give 1:1000 time odds to the human chess champion having classical time control, and be on par with him. [1] There was previously a bug in the web version that allowed you to appear as if you were playing against the bot on level 25 when you were actually playing it on level 1. It looks like they removed the engine level bots entirely from the web version. It’s still available in the mobile app. By the way, the estimated ratings at the other levels are definitely inflated. I was able to beat the level 22 (2600) engine with some consistency. That one’s supposed to be grandmaster level, but as you can see from my credentials, that’s far from my actual playing strength. EDIT: The engine used for the bots is actually Komodo, not Stockfish, but the same applied. It should essentially be unplayable at the strongest setting.

Name: Håkon Hapnes Strand
Question: A host of tech companies, like Twitter, Meta, Lyft and Stripe, have recently announced hiring freezes or job cuts. Why are we seeing this sudden wave of tech layoffs?
Answer: The market for tech stocks has crashed. We haven't seen a recession in tech this bad since the financial crisis of 2008, or perhaps even since the dot-com bubble burst at the turn of the century. Why has this happened? That's too complicated to explain in a single sentence. Some of the dynamics involved are so complicated that we don't fully understand them. The stock market is a complex beast. But it's probably not wrong to say that it has to do with macroeconomic effects resulting from the Covid-19 pandemic and the war in Ukraine. In any case, trillions of dollars in value has been shaved off. The inevitable consequence of such a dramatic downswing is that companies need to lay off large numbers of employees in order to manage costs and avoid bankruptcies. I can tell you from first-hand experience that the downswing is also affecting unlisted startups seeking investors. During a recession like this, VC funding dries up. As a result, we've had to lay off a number of people too.
